To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

we have isolated human antibodies that neutralize the complement‐regulating proteins CD55 and 59 and that, by doing so, they increase the complement‐mediating cytotoxic activity of the anti‐CD20 antibody Rituximab.

the two human antibodies MB‐59 and MB‐55, produced by recombinant technology and specific to the complement‐regulating proteins CD55 and 59, respectively, are capable of neutralizing the inhibitory activity on complement‐mediated cell cytoxic activity exerted by these proteins.
we have developed two human monoclonal miniantibodies that neutralize the inhibitory activity on complement of CD55 and of CD59.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the identification of novel therapeutic agents for cancer.
the development of novel therapeutic strategies for the treatment of lymphoma.
the use of human antibodies against complement‐regulatory protein to enhance the efficacy of the complement‐dependent cytotoxicity induced by monoclonal antibody‐based therapy.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the two MB, MB‐55 and ‐59, represent a therapeutic tool that may be used in the treatment of lymphoma, and other tumors that express the two CRP, to increase the complement dependent cytotoxicity of Rituximac, and other anti‐CD20 antibodies.
these human antibodies may represent a therapeutic approach to increase the complement dependent cytotoxic activity of monoclonal antibodies in the treatment of B‐cell non‐Hodkin's lymphoma.
MB‐55 and/or MB‐59 may be used as a complementation tool to increase the killing activity of Rituzimab in the therapy of non-Hodgkin's Lymphoma.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we have isolated two human antibodies that can neutralize the inhibitory activity exerted on complement activation by two of the complement‐inhibitory molecules, CD55 and 59.
the two human monoclonal miniantibodies MB‐55 and ‐59, specific for the complement‐regulators CD55 and CD 59, respectively, may represent a new tool for the treatment of non-Hodgkin's Lymphoma.

the use of human antibodies that neutralize the activity of CD55/CD59 can be exploited to enhance the complement‐dependent cell‐killing activity of chimeric or human monoclonal antibody‐based therapies.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the two human monoclonal anti‐CD55 and anti‐CD59 antibodies can be used to increase the complement activation induced by RituximAb in the treatment of lymphoma.

we have isolated two human monoclonal antibody fragments against the complement‐regulating proteins (CRP), CD55 (also known as DAF) and CD59 (also known as protectin), from a phage‐display human antibody library.
we have developed a novel therapeutic tool for increasing the killing activity of Rituzumab in the treatment non‐Hodkin's lymphoma, a type of cancer that is treated by Rituximb.
